openItems.explanation: Alder Point’s schedule counts pending change order PCO-14, $640,000.00 for the MRI suite shielding redesign, submitted August 28 and not signed by the owner. It adds $259,200.00 to the quarter’s revenue and gross profit, 259% of materiality. Revenue from an unapproved change order may be counted only when it is probable that a significant reversal will not occur. The CPA reads the change order, the owner’s and architect’s correspondence and the history of approvals on this owner, and decides. The machine counts nothing either way.

Interest is recorded when Cinderbrook Bank debits it, not as it accrues. September’s interest, $35,350.00 on the bank’s statement, is not in the books, and June’s $28,665.00 was recorded in July. Expense for the quarter is understated $6,685.00, 6.7% of materiality, and accrued interest by $35,350.00. Proposed: debit interest expense $6,685.00 and partners’ capital $28,665.00 (June’s interest, a correction of FY2026, if the CPA treats it so), credit 2410 accrued interest $35,350.00. Under performance materiality: passed if the client declines. The machine never posts.

Tangible net worth as the loan agreement defines it is $6,629,999.00, $129,999.00 above the $6,500,000 minimum, after leaving out $715,500.00 due from Juniper Ridge Partners, an affiliate. With INT-01 recorded and PCO-14 left out it would be $6,335,449.00, short by $164,551.00: an event of default unless the bank waives it, which could make the line of credit and the term loan current. Working capital $4,789,499.00 and leverage 2.46 to 1 stay within their limits either way. The controller says the certificate goes to the bank by November 14 (Q11). The CPA decides REV-01 first, then the covenant and the debt classification.

The Juniper Ridge Partners job (J-2625), nine flex units, is built for Juniper Ridge Partners LLC, a commercial developer under the same owners, building flex industrial units on land it owns (Q7). It earned $1,638,000.00 of revenue in the quarter, and $715,500.00 is due from it in receivables, retainage and underbillings. The interim statements fold it into contract receivables and have no related party note. The CPA decides the disclosure; the bonding company and the lender read these statements.

Tideflats Cold Storage’s estimate rose from $16,284,000.00 to $17,480,000.00 (14 tilt-up panels recast, a 9% panel price increase; Q3). The cumulative effect, $382,720.00 below the June margin, is in this quarter, which is how a change in estimate is recorded. The job still expects a profit, so no loss provision. The backcharge against the precaster is not recorded, which is right while it is only a claim. The CPA reads the revised estimate and the recast quotes.

The controller answered in writing that interest on both loans is accrued monthly (Q5). The bank’s statement and the books show it is not. Every other answer was corroborated by a record. The CPA considers what this means for relying on the answers and asks how the controller closes the quarter.

After the quarter, HGC drew a further $500,000.00 on the line of credit on October 9 and started Lakeside Clinic (Q9). Neither changes the September 30 figures; the CPA decides whether the statements should mention the borrowing.

Materiality is proposed at $100,000.00, 0.5% of the quarter’s revenue, with performance materiality $75,000.00, clearly trivial $5,000.00 and a $50,000.00 threshold for investigating a change. The engagement partner sets the final amounts.
No management representation letter has been obtained. A review needs one, dated near the date of the CPA’s report, covering the answers relied on here.

These are draft workpapers and a draft review memo for the engagement partner. They are not a review report and express no conclusion. Nothing has been signed, posted or sent to the client, the bank or the bonding company.
